formulas.name: Mass-energy equivalence
formulas.explanation: Einstein showed that mass is a form of energy: a mass m at rest contains energy mc². Because c² is enormous, a tiny amount of mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy. Nuclear reactions release energy because the products have slightly less mass than the reactants.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for nuclear fission and fusion, particle physics, and the energy of the Sun.
assumptions: m is the rest mass (for moving objects use the relativistic energy)

example.story: How much energy is equivalent to 1 gram of mass?
steps: E ≈ 9.0 × 10¹³ J, about the energy of a 20 kiloton explosion

formulas.name: Radioactive decay law

variables.name: nuclei remaining
variables.description: Number of undecayed nuclei at time t.

variables.name: decay constant
variables.description: Probability per second that a nucleus decays.

formulas.explanation: Each nucleus has the same small chance of decaying each second, independent of the others and of its age. So the number that decay is proportional to the number left, which gives exponential decay. The same law describes activity and mass of a radioactive sample.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for radioactive sources, carbon dating, medical tracers and nuclear waste.
assumptions: large number of nuclei (the law is statistical)

example.story: A sample has 1 000 000 radioactive nuclei with decay constant 0.1 s⁻¹. How many remain after 10 s?

formulas.name: Half-life and decay constant

variables.name: half-life
variables.description: Time for half the nuclei to decay.

formulas.explanation: The half-life is the time after which half of the nuclei remain. Setting N = N₀/2 in N = N₀e^(-λt) gives e^(-λt) = ½, so t = ln 2 / λ. A short half-life means a large decay constant and a very active source.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to convert between half-life and decay constant, for example in dating and medical physics.

example.story: Iodine-131 used in medicine has a half-life of 8.02 days (692 928 s). What is its decay constant?

formulas.name: Amount remaining after a number of half-lives

variables.name: amount remaining
variables.description: Nuclei, mass or activity left (same unit as N₀).

variables.name: time
variables.description: Time elapsed (any unit, the same as the half-life).

formulas.explanation: Every half-life the amount halves, so after t/t½ half-lives it has been multiplied by ½ that many times. This form is equivalent to the exponential decay law and is often easier to use with half-lives given in years.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for decay problems stated in half-lives, such as how much of a sample is left after some years.
assumptions: t and t½ in the same unit

example.story: A sample contains 80 g of an isotope with a half-life of 5 years. How much is left after 15 years?

formulas.name: Activity of a radioactive source

variables.name: activity
variables.description: Decays per second (1 becquerel = 1 decay per second).

formulas.explanation: If each nucleus decays with probability λ per second, then N nuclei produce on average λN decays per second. Activity therefore falls with the same half-life as the number of nuclei.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find how active a source is, or how many radioactive atoms it contains.

example.story: A source contains 5 × 10¹² nuclei with λ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ s⁻¹. What is its activity?

formulas.name: Photoelectric equation

variables.name: maximum kinetic energy
variables.description: Kinetic energy of the fastest emitted electrons.

variables.name: work function
variables.description: Minimum energy to free an electron from the metal (2.28 eV for sodium).

formulas.explanation: Light knocks electrons out of a metal one photon at a time. Each photon gives its energy hf to a single electron; part of it (the work function φ) is needed to escape, and the rest is kinetic energy. Brighter light gives more electrons, but only higher frequency gives faster ones, which convinced Einstein that light comes in quanta.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for photocells, solar panels, photomultipliers and the photoelectric effect experiment.
assumptions: one photon frees at most one electron
if hf < φ no electrons are emitted

example.story: Ultraviolet light of frequency 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz shines on sodium (φ = 2.28 eV = 3.653 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). What is the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons?

formulas.name: Threshold frequency

variables.name: threshold frequency
variables.description: Lowest frequency that can release electrons.

variables.name: work function
variables.description: Minimum energy to free an electron.

formulas.explanation: Below the threshold frequency a photon does not have enough energy to free an electron, however bright the light. At exactly f₀ the photon energy equals the work function and the electrons escape with zero kinetic energy.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find which colours of light can cause photoemission from a given metal.

example.story: What is the threshold frequency for sodium, with a work function of 3.653 × 10⁻¹⁹ J?

formulas.name: Photon emitted in an energy level transition

variables.name: photon frequency
variables.description: Frequency of the emitted (or absorbed) light.

variables.name: upper level energy
variables.description: Energy of the higher level (often negative).

formulas.explanation: Electrons in atoms can only have certain energies. When an electron drops to a lower level, the atom emits one photon carrying exactly the energy difference. This is why each element has its own pattern of sharp spectral lines.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for emission and absorption spectra, lasers, LEDs and fluorescent lights.

example.story: An electron drops from a level at -2.42 × 10⁻¹⁹ J to one at -5.45 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the frequency of the emitted photon?
steps: f ≈ 4.57 × 10¹⁴ Hz (red light, the hydrogen alpha line)

formulas.name: Energy levels of hydrogen (Bohr model)

variables.name: energy of level n
variables.description: Energy of the electron in level n (zero means just free).

variables.name: principal quantum number
variables.description: Level number: 1 for the ground state, 2, 3, ...

formulas.explanation: In Bohr's model the electron in hydrogen can only occupy levels with energy -13.6 eV / n². The energies are negative because the electron is bound: 13.6 eV is needed to remove it from the ground state. The levels crowd together as n grows.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for hydrogen spectra, ionisation energy and the photon energies of transitions.
assumptions: infinitely heavy nucleus (the reduced-mass correction is about 0.05 %)

example.story: What is the energy of the n = 2 level of hydrogen?

formulas.name: Rydberg formula

variables.name: lower level
variables.description: Level the electron falls to (2 for the Balmer series).

variables.name: upper level
variables.description: Level the electron falls from (larger than n₁).

formulas.explanation: Dividing the energy difference between two Bohr levels by hc gives the wavenumber of the emitted light. Rydberg found this pattern in hydrogen's spectrum before quantum theory explained it. Falling to n₁ = 1 gives ultraviolet lines (Lyman), to n₁ = 2 visible lines (Balmer).
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to predict or identify hydrogen spectral lines.
assumptions: infinite nuclear mass, so hydrogen's real lines are about 0.05 % longer

example.story: What is the wavelength of the red Balmer line, from n = 3 to n = 2?
steps: λ ≈ 656.1 nm; the reduced-mass correction gives 656.5 nm in vacuum (656.3 nm in air)

formulas.name: Lorentz factor

variables.name: Lorentz factor
variables.description: How strongly relativity changes time, length and energy (1 at rest).

variables.name: speed
variables.description: Speed relative to the observer (less than c).

formulas.explanation: The Lorentz factor appears in every formula of special relativity. It is almost exactly 1 at everyday speeds and grows without limit as v approaches the speed of light. At 87 % of c it is 2, so moving clocks run at half speed.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for time dilation, length contraction, and relativistic energy and momentum.

example.story: What is the Lorentz factor for a spacecraft moving at 0.8c (2.398 × 10⁸ m/s)?

formulas.name: Time dilation

variables.name: dilated time
variables.description: Time interval measured by the observer who sees the clock moving.

variables.name: proper time
variables.description: Time interval measured by a clock moving with the event.

formulas.explanation: A moving clock runs slow compared with clocks at rest. Light bouncing between mirrors in a moving clock travels a longer, diagonal path, and since light's speed is the same for everyone, each tick takes longer. Muons from cosmic rays reach the ground only because their decay is slowed this way.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for fast particles, GPS satellite clock corrections and the twin paradox.

example.story: Muons live 2.2 µs at rest. How long do they live, as measured from the ground, when moving at 0.99c?

formulas.name: Length contraction

variables.name: contracted length
variables.description: Length measured by an observer who sees the object moving.

variables.name: proper length
variables.description: Length measured at rest relative to the object.

formulas.explanation: A moving object is shorter along its direction of motion, as measured by an observer it passes. The effect is the partner of time dilation and keeps the speed of light the same for all observers. Lengths across the motion are not affected.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for fast-moving objects and particles, and for the muon's view of the atmosphere.
assumptions: only the length along the motion contracts

example.story: A 100 m spaceship passes a space station at 0.6c (1.799 × 10⁸ m/s). How long does it look to the station?

formulas.name: Total relativistic energy
formulas.explanation: The total energy of a moving particle is its rest energy mc² multiplied by the Lorentz factor. The kinetic energy is (γ - 1)mc², which reduces to ½mv² at low speed. Because γ grows without limit near c, no massive particle can reach the speed of light.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for particle accelerators, cosmic rays and electrons in high-voltage devices.

example.story: What is the total energy of an electron (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving at 0.6c?

formulas.name: Relativistic momentum
formulas.explanation: At high speeds the ordinary momentum mv is not conserved in collisions; γmv is. It agrees with mv at everyday speeds and grows without limit as v approaches c.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for fast particles in accelerators and magnetic spectrometers, and in the energy-momentum relation.

example.story: What is the momentum of an electron moving at 0.6c?

formulas.name: Energy-momentum relation
formulas.explanation: Energy, momentum and mass of any particle are linked like the sides of a right-angled triangle. For a particle at rest it gives E = mc²; for a massless photon E = pc. Particle physicists use it to find masses from measured energies and momenta.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it whenever you know two of energy, momentum and mass, from photons to particle collisions.

example.story: An electron (9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg) has momentum 5.0 × 10⁻²² kg·m/s. What is its total energy?

formulas.name: Momentum of a photon
formulas.explanation: Even though photons have no mass, they carry momentum, which is why light exerts a tiny pressure. A photon's momentum is its energy divided by c, or h over its wavelength. Solar sails use this push.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for radiation pressure, solar sails, optical tweezers and Compton scattering.

example.story: What momentum does a 500 nm photon carry?

formulas.name: Compton scattering

variables.name: scattering angle
variables.description: Angle the photon is deflected through, in radians.

formulas.explanation: When an X-ray photon bounces off a free electron, it gives the electron some energy and comes away with a longer wavelength. Treating the collision like billiard balls with photon momentum h/λ gives this shift. Compton's 1923 experiment showed that photons carry momentum.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it for X-ray and gamma-ray scattering, medical imaging and radiation shielding.
assumptions: the electron is free and initially at rest

example.story: An X-ray photon is scattered through 90 degrees by a free electron. By how much does its wavelength increase?

formulas.name: Heisenberg uncertainty principle (minimum)
formulas.explanation: Quantum mechanics forbids knowing both the position and the momentum of a particle exactly. The product of their uncertainties is at least ħ/2; the equation here gives that smallest possible value. It is not a flaw of instruments but a property of nature, and it explains why electrons do not fall into the nucleus.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate minimum momenta or energies of confined particles, such as an electron in an atom.
assumptions: the equality gives the minimum; real states usually exceed it

example.story: An electron is confined to a region 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m wide, about the size of an atom. What is the smallest possible uncertainty in its momentum?

formulas.name: Nuclear radius

variables.name: radius constant
variables.description: About 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m (1.2 fm), from scattering experiments.

formulas.explanation: Nucleons pack together at roughly constant density, so the volume of a nucleus is proportional to the number of nucleons A. Radius goes as the cube root of volume, hence A^(1/3). All nuclei have about the same enormous density, around 2 × 10¹⁷ kg/m³.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to estimate nuclear sizes and densities, or closest approach in scattering experiments.
assumptions: r₀ between 1.2 and 1.25 fm depending on the experiment

example.story: Estimate the radius of an aluminium-27 nucleus.

formulas.name: Nuclear binding energy from mass defect

variables.name: binding energy
variables.description: Energy needed to separate the nucleus into its nucleons.

variables.name: mass defect
variables.description: Mass of the separate nucleons minus the mass of the nucleus.

formulas.explanation: A nucleus weighs less than the protons and neutrons that make it up. The missing mass, the mass defect, is the binding energy divided by c². Nuclei near iron have the most binding energy per nucleon, which is why both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones release energy.
formulas.whenToUse: Use it to find binding energies and the energy released in nuclear reactions.

example.story: A helium-4 nucleus has a mass defect of 5.0442 × 10⁻²⁹ kg. What is its binding energy?
